data.title: Holiday Shoppers Lean on Grocery Loyalty Programs to Save In 2026
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Shoppers would rather cut back on holiday clothing, décor or events than scale back their holiday meal, and 36% want loyalty member discounts to make Thanksgiving prep easier.
  • While 72% of shoppers say their store’s loyalty program is essential to saving, only 58% of shoppers earning under $35,000 are members, compared with 78% of those earning $150,000 or more.

As families prepare for the holidays this season, the centerpiece of the season remains the family holiday meal. And food shoppers are taking steps protect it in the current challenging economic environment, according to The Food Industry Association (FMI).

The U.S. Grocery Shopper Trends 2026: Holidays report from FMI found 45% of shoppers are extremely or very concerned about rising prices for holiday foods, up eight percentage points from a year earlier. Yet shoppers say they would rather cut back on holiday clothing, décor or events than scale back their holiday feast, turning to their grocery store’s loyalty program to make the math work.

When asked how grocers can make Thanksgiving prep easier, the top request is holiday discounts for loyalty program members (36%), followed by special displays for the holiday meal (29%) and for specific dishes (25%).

How Confident Are Shoppers About Their Grocery Budgets This Holiday Season?

The FMI’s U.S. Grocery Shopper Sentiment Index stands at 72 this fall, near its historical high.

“Food is what holds the holidays together, and shoppers are telling us they will protect the holiday meal even if it means trimming elsewhere,” said Leslie G. Sarasin, president and CEO, FMI , in a statement. “Concern about grocery prices remains high, but it has eased slightly since August, and the share of shoppers who feel in control of their grocery spending has climbed 13 points over the same period. In fact, for the first time since we began tracking holiday trends in August 2024, shoppers feel more in control of their grocery budgets than of their other major household expenses.”

How Are AI and Scratch Cooking Shaping Thanksgiving Meals in 2026?

The Thanksgiving and holiday dinners are being joined by AI in the kitchen this year. Weekly AI use among shoppers rose to 27% from 19% a year ago, and 65% would like to use AI to help plan holiday meals, most often to find new recipes (34%) or festive ideas (27%).

Among shoppers planning a turkey, 59% will make it from scratch at home, up 16 points from 2025, while freshly prepared turkey fell 10 points to 19%. Turkey (68%), mashed potatoes (63%), stuffing (62%) and a warm vegetable side (50%) all rose versus last year. Where at least one Thanksgiving dish is homemade, 95% of shoppers plan to help prepare the meal, and nearly as many are excited about the prep (90%) as the holiday itself (89%).

As they shopped for their Thanksgiving day meal, 24% are extremely or very concerned about holiday food out-of-stocks. But half said they would simply make a different familiar dish and 35% would try a new recipe.

Why Are Grocery Loyalty Programs Essential for Holiday Savings?

The report shows grocery loyalty programs are one of the most practical tools shoppers have for saving money this season. Of shoppers surveyed, 72% strongly or somewhat agree that their primary store’s loyalty program is essential to helping them save on groceries and stay within their budgets. Key attraction for loyalty programs include:

  • Members find real value, mostly through savings. When a program is offered, 71% of shoppers join, and 95% of members find their program at least somewhat valuable. Shoppers value the money-saving benefits most— general everyday savings and discounts (95%), personalized savings and discounts (91%), points to use on a variety of items (90%) and gas savings or points (86%).
  • Loyalty members enjoy shopping more. Shoppers who see their loyalty program as essential rate their primary store higher (85% vs. 79%) and are more likely to love or like grocery shopping (50% vs. 37%).
  • Demand outpaces access, and those who could save the most are missing out. Among shoppers whose primary store doesn’t offer a loyalty program, 68% are extremely or very interested in having one. Where programs exist, only 58% of shoppers earning under $35,000 are members, compared with 78% of those earning $150,000 or more.

“Loyalty programs are delivering exactly what shoppers need right now: everyday savings that help them stay on budget without giving up the holiday meals they love,” Sarasin said. “The opportunity ahead is making sure all shoppers, especially those in lower-income households and younger consumers, know these savings are available and find them easy to use.”

The full U.S. Grocery Shopper Trends 2026: Holidays report can be downloaded by clicking here.

data.title: The Last Mile Starts in the Warehouse: Why Fulfillment Visibility Is the Key to Omnichannel Success
data.description:
On the surface, last-mile delivery issues look like shipping problems. An order arrives late, a retailer flags a compliance violation or the wrong product arrives. The first instinct is to look at the carrier, but the root cause often lies within the fulfillment warehouse, where inventory, order management, processes and technology converge.

For omnichannel brands, this distinction matters. A delayed shipment can disappoint a customer, but a retail order that misses routing requirements or arrives with incorrect labeling can trigger chargebacks, jeopardize retailer relationships and put future business at risk. As a brand grows, the margin for operational errors shrinks.

The way to solve this is with greater visibility into fulfillment operations. With it, teams can determine whether an order is ready to ship correctly in the first place. A brand’s fulfillment provider should provide that visibility.

Why Fulfillment Is Overlooked in the Last Mile

Fulfillment is often treated as the step between receiving products and handing an order to a carrier. In reality, it’s one of the most complex stages of the supply chain.

To ensure an order arrives to the customer on time and as promised, it’s critical that inventory is recorded accurately, available quantities synchronized across sales channels, and orders picked, packed and labeled according to the specific retailer’s requirements. Each step depends on the accuracy of the one before it. A receiving discrepancy can lead to an inaccurate inventory count, while a picking or labeling error can turn an otherwise complete order into a costly compliance issue.

The warehouse or distribution center is the last opportunity to detect and correct these errors before a shipment enters the transportation network. After that, correcting a mistake becomes more difficult and expensive. For retail orders, the consequences can extend beyond an individual shipment compliance penalty and become a strained business relationship. Fulfillment is a crucial control point for protecting both the customer experience and the retail economics of an omnichannel business.

Visibility Is the Solution

Delivery issues can often be addressed earlier with better visibility into fulfillment operations. Too many brands still rely on tracking numbers or spreadsheets to confirm that an order has shipped. While these tools provide a snapshot of activity, they may not explain where a problem is occurring.

Meaningful operational visibility goes further. Brands need timely access to inventory levels, inbound receiving, open orders and shipment status, along with the ability to identify discrepancies without requesting a report or waiting for a warehouse contact to respond.

Teams having access to the same operational information enables small discrepancies to be addressed before they become a major disruption. It’s important that brands investigate an inventory mismatch before it affects a customer order. Likewise, a delayed inbound shipment can be identified before it creates a stockout.

Today’s modern and complex supply chain requires connected systems to provide data across the brand, its fulfillment partner and its sales channels, reducing the blind spots that emerge when each function operates independently. Visibility won’t eliminate every exception, but it can help teams detect, understand and resolve issues sooner.

Direct EDI: Connecting Retail Orders to Execution

Retail fulfillment adds a layer of complexity. Retailers have specific requirements for purchase orders, routing, shipping windows, labels and advance shipment notifications.

Electronic data interchange (EDI) enables businesses to exchange standardized documents electronically, translating retailer requirements into information that trading partners’ systems can process. But having EDI capability alone isn’t enough. The integration quality and ongoing management are equally important.

Disconnected systems, manual intervention and delayed messages can leave orders or exceptions unnoticed until a shipment misses its window. Direct EDI integration can reduce intermediary handoffs, while a well-managed EDI service helps ensure that document mapping, testing, monitoring and exception resolution are handled consistently.

The goal isn’t simply to connect systems. It’s also to ensure that retailer requirements reach the fulfillment operation accurately and that order and shipment information flows back to the relevant systems promptly. Integrating EDI with warehouse processes gives teams more time to address problems before they become chargebacks, missed delivery windows or rejected shipments.

Make Retail Compliance Part of the Workflow

One common mistake is treating retail compliance as a final checklist rather than an operational discipline. By the time a shipment reaches the loading dock, many important decisions have already been made. It’s important to build retail requirements into fulfillment workflows, with the right routing guidance, labeling, documentation and verification steps in place before orders leave the facility.

The same principle applies to inventory accuracy. Brands need reliable information about what is physically present, what is available to promise and what has already been committed. Without that foundation, even sophisticated order-routing technology can make poor decisions.

Choosing a third-party logistics (3PL) partner, therefore requires more than comparing shipping rates or warehouse capacity. Brands should understand how a prospective partner manages retail integrations, monitors exceptions, verifies orders and provides access to operational data. A capable partner helps identify risks and resolve issues proactively, rather than simply reporting what went wrong after a shipment leaves the building.

Takeaway: Fix the Process Before the Package Ships

Last-mile performance is shaped long before a carrier collects a package. Accurate inventory, connected systems, disciplined warehouse execution and timely information all influence whether an order reaches its destination correctly and on time.

As omnichannel brands grow, complexity can quickly rise. New retailers introduce new requirements, while higher order volumes can overwhelm manual workarounds that once seemed manageable. Without repeatable processes and reliable information, small problems can multiply into expensive bottlenecks.

Brands should evaluate whether their systems provide timely visibility across channels, whether retail requirements are built into fulfillment workflows and whether exceptions can be identified and resolved quickly.

Fulfillment visibility should be treated as a foundational capability, not just a reporting feature. Direct EDI integration, well-designed warehouse workflows and accessible operational data give teams more opportunities to catch discrepancies early and protect retail compliance.

No technology can prevent every mistake, and no integration replaces sound operational processes. But when information moves reliably between systems, teams can intervene before problems become expensive. The most effective last-mile strategy may begin by looking upstream.

With over 20 years of finance, sales, operations, and leadership experience, Dave Tu has led DCL during a transformational time of growth, taking the company from a regional logistics operator to a national domestic provider. He leads with a tech-forward mindset, often investing in new operational tech (robotics, automation, green energy) to give DCL’s customers the best possible market advantage in the ever-shifting ecommerce landscape.
data.author: Dave Tu, President, DCL Logistics

data.title: 5 Ways Small Businesses Can Make Holiday Packages More Memorable
data.description:
Consider a customer who discovers your business online while holiday shopping. They may spend twenty minutes comparing some products, reading about your story, and placing their first order. A few days later, a plain brown box arrives on their porch containing the product and a packing slip. The product itself is excellent, but the experience of receiving it is indistinguishable from every other package delivered that week.

Small businesses can benefit from giving special attention to packaging, particularly during the fourth quarter. Holiday shoppers are often first-time buyers, prompted by a recommendation, a gift guide, or a search result. The package is the first physical object that business places in the customer’s hands, and it arrives at the only point in the transaction where a brand has the customer’s full attention and final evaluation.. Making your package memorable provides an unspoken advantage.

Most small businesses treat packaging as a line item in shipping costs, but approached deliberately, it functions as a marketing channel the customer has already agreed to receive. Here is where and why that investment pays off.

Begin with the Exterior

The outside of the box does the most work, which makes it one of the easiest ways for a small business to showcase their brand this season. It is what the customer sees on the doorstep, what sits on the kitchen counter while they find scissors, and what appears in the background if they photograph the contents.

Improving it does not require a massive (or expensive) overhaul. A branded sticker sealing a plain mailer accomplishes most of what a printed box does at a fraction of the cost. Custom packing tape delivers similar consistency on every order without requiring a significant volume commitment. For businesses that do invest in printed mailers, the more practical approach is to order one or two sizes used most often rather than a full range that will sit in storage until spring.

Treat the Interior as Part of the Product

Opening a box to find a product loose among packing peanuts communicates to a customer that presentation doesn’t matter, their order was one of many hastily packed and shipped. On the other hand, opening a package to find the product gift-wrapped in tissue paper and sealed with a sticker shows thoughtfulness and taste, and the cost difference is measured in cents per order.

Tissue paper, crinkle fill in a brand color, or a simple wrap-and-seal treatment introduces a brief pause between opening the box and reaching the product. That pause is the entire mechanism at work. It signals that someone considered and hand-wrapped this particular order, which remains one of the clearest distinctions and advantages between a small business and a fulfillment warehouse.

Add a Personal Signature Where it Counts

The most effective insert available to most small businesses costs nothing but time: a brief handwritten note.

It does not need to be long, and it should not be a form letter reproduced by hand. One or two lines referencing the specific order, the color selected, the likelihood that it is a gift, or the hope that it arrives on schedule or that the customer likes it, contributes more to customer retention than a comparable spend on acquisition.

Holiday volume can make this difficult to sustain across every order, and that constraint is worth planning around rather than abandoning the practice altogether. Reserving handwritten notes for first-time customers or for orders above a set value preserves most of the effect at a manageable workload. Where handwriting is genuinely impractical, printed note cards carrying a signature and a single handwritten line perform nearly just as well.

Give Every Package a Second Purpose

Each box shipped represents a delivery vehicle already paid for. Most businesses will send it out carrying nothing beyond the product itself.

A little something extra changes that calculation. Including a discount code redeemable in January is the familiar version, and it works precisely because it reaches the customer at the moment they are most favorably disposed toward the business. Other options are worth considering as well: a referral card the recipient can pass along, care instructions that reduce return rates, a percent off their next order, a QR code linking to a gift guide or exchange form, or a brief card explaining the business’s mission and values.

That final example carries more weight than it initially appears to. During the holidays, a substantial share of the people opening a business’s packages are not its customers. They are people its customers care about. Introducing the brand to that audience costs one printed card and reaches them at a moment of genuine goodwill.

Design the Set, Not the Pieces

The four tactics above are worth considerably more in combination than in isolation, and only when they share a cohesive visual language.

The discipline here mirrors what applies to storefront signage and direct mail: one color palette, one typeface pairing, one simple motif, applied consistently across every element. The sticker, the tissue paper, the note card, and the insert should read as a coordinated set. When they do, a customer ordering again in March recognizes the package before reading the label. When they do not, the packaging reads as an assortment of unrelated promotional purchases, which leaves a weaker impression than a plain box would have.

Achieving this does not require a design budget or outside help. It requires selecting a palette and a motif once, documenting them, and holding to those choices when the next order goes in during the November rush.

Measure Packaging Against the Next Order

There is a natural tendency to evaluate packaging against the transaction it accompanies, where it registers as pure expense. The return does not appear on that line. It appears in January, when a customer who received something that left an impression returns to the site directly instead of browsing competitors’ offerings.

Holiday volume represents the single moment in the year when a small business introduces itself to a large number of people simultaneously, most of whom may never encounter its advertising. What arrives on their doorstep is that introduction. A few dollars and some advance planning determine resonance and repeat purchases.

Erin Shea is the Senior Director of North America Marketing at VistaPrint. VistaPrint helps small business owners and entrepreneurs create custom designs and professional marketing.
data.author: Erin Shea, Senior Director of North America Marketing, VistaPrint

data.title: AI Plans Outrun Store Realities as Bad Stock Data Cost Retailers Millions
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Store associates say stock data matches the shelf just 46% of the time, and a retailer with 10,000 associates faces more than $41 million a year in labor costs to compensate.
  • Associates who took part in technology pilots used most store tools at a 74% rate and were twice as likely to report high trust in stock data as associates who were never asked for input.

Global research from Scandit reveals retail’s race to deploy AI is running ahead of the data reality inside its stores as associates reported that stock information matches what they find on the shelf just 46% of the time while only 8% trust store data completely.

This creates a costly gap between what the system says, what is actually in the store and what customers experience, while leaving AI and other technology investments to act on incomplete records. That gap is already being absorbed by labor as associates estimate they would each get back more than 4.4 hours a week, nearly six working weeks a year, if they had data they could trust.

A retailer employing 10,000 store associates, for example, faces more than $41 million a year in labor cost tied to compensating for the gap.

Is Retail’s AI Problem Really a Store Data Problem?

Retailers do not have an AI adoption problem as much as a store truth problem,” said Samuel Mueller, CEO and co-founder of Scandit.

“Associates are spending valuable time repairing these gaps, yet much of that work disappears into unofficial tracking systems,” said Mueller in a statement. “Before retailers ask AI to make more decisions based on inaccurate store data, they need a shared, accurate view of what is actually happening on the shelf and across their stores.”

What Is a “Shadow Store” in Retail?

The result is a ‘shadow store’ in which vital information exists outside the record that head office, dashboards and AI systems rely on. When the system is wrong, associates do what they have to do to keep the store running. Nearly half (49%) correct the record themselves and 44% raise a stock adjustment. But among associates who take action, 42% bypass the official system entirely, while 68% use at least one informal method, including paper notes, team chats, personal phone photos and apps or memory.

Associates’ trust in stock data does not build gradually. The survey highlights it stays low until the data is very good as only 8% of associates completely trust their store’s stock information, and only one in four say it is accurate more than 70% of the time.

Among associates who put accuracy anywhere up to 50%, roughly a quarter report high trust, and that figure barely moves until accuracy passes 70%, when it rises sharply.

How Does Inaccurate Stock Data Affect Customers and Technology Adoption?

The consequences extend beyond productivity. Associates report spending an average of 4.1 hours each week handling customer questions that store technology should be able to answer, and are asked to physically check whether an item is in stock 5.85 times a week on average. More than one in five say they make those checks more than ten times a week.

The findings point to a practical lesson for technology deployment: associates who participated in a pilot reported using most store tools at a rate of 74%, compared with 61% among those who were consulted before rollout and those who were never asked. Half of pilot participants reported high trust in their stock data, compared with 25% of those who were never asked for input.

Read The Store Truth Gap report here.

data.title: The Holiday Shopping Battle Is Moving to AI.  Are Retailers Ready?
data.description:
There’s no way around the unpleasant truth: Traditional e-commerce has devolved into a fragmented, broken process. Today, when a consumer wants new headphones, for instance, they start with an ad-cluttered search engine, visit a favorite retail website, or maybe get recommendations from friends. Then they open a dozen browser tabs, dive into product specs, check reviews, and hunt for discount codes before deciding what to buy. It’s an exhausting, time-wasting process that leads many consumers to just give up or pay more because they don’t want to deal with the hassles.

As the 2026 holiday season arrives, that process just won’t cut it – for merchants or consumers. Today, a growing number of shoppers are turning to AI. They’re telling shopping assistants what they’re looking for, what they’re willing to spend, and which features matter most. Then they’ll ask it to narrow choices, compare prices, and help them decide where to buy quickly. In 2026, this isn’t your father’s (or mother’s) holiday shopping season.

This is a significant change, because much of the work prior to a purchase takes place before the shopper visits the website. According to Accenture’s 2026 holiday shopping research, nearly two-thirds of U.S. shoppers expect AI to influence at least 30% of their holiday spending. Finding deals is the top use case at 40%, followed by comparing products at 31% and deciding where to shop at 30%. These aren’t casual browsers looking for gift inspiration. They’re using AI to make decisions that retailers have traditionally worked hard to influence: which products deserve consideration, which product offers represent good value, and which merchant gets the sale.

It All Starts with a Conversation

For years, the traditional online buying journey started with keywords. The consumer typed in “best women’s running shoes” or a particular brand and model and looked at pages of results. Conversational shopping rewires that process and lets the consumer get more specific: “I need running shoes for someone with wide feet who runs three times a week, mostly on pavement. My budget is $120.”

The AI shopping assistant uses those details about fit, use, and budget to quickly narrow the options to a small list of likely choices. For retailers, this changes what it means to be “discoverable.” A product page might perform well for conventional searches by matching a popular keyword.

But when an AI assistant works on a detailed request, the quality and completeness of your product information become crucial. Does the listing describe the fit? Are specifications available? Is the price current? Can the shopper confidently determine the product will arrive on time? These are practical questions, not abstract concerns. No retailer can guarantee a place in an AI-generated recommendation, but accurate, detailed product information gives shopping tools a better foundation to understand what a retailer sells.

Making the Shortlist May Matter More than Ranking First

Retailers have spent years jockeying for prominent positions on search engine results pages, shopping ads, and online marketplaces. Those positions still matter. But AI introduces another challenge: how do you make the cut and get on the small list of products a shopper will seriously consider?

For example, suppose a consumer wants a coffee maker for less than $150. Hundreds of products meet that threshold. So when an AI assistant narrows those choices to four or five, many brands and models may never get a look. Getting onto that shortlist is a must.

That’s why it’s important to think beyond product titles and promotional descriptions. A shopper may care about how easy a coffee maker is to clean, whether it fits in kitchen cabinets, or whether replacement parts are available. Those details can distinguish one product from another.

Comparison Shopping Retains its Central Role

The dominant role of pricing isn’t going away, of course. What’s going away is the hassle required to compare offers. Previously, a shopper comparing the same television on five different websites had to juggle prices, promotions, shipping charges, delivery dates, and even cash back. AI-assisted shopping quickly brings all of those factors into one clean comparison and a ranked set of recommendations.

But don’t be fooled. That doesn’t mean the buyer’s journey simply becomes a margin-destroying race to the bottom. Discerning customers value other aspects of the purchase – such as shipping speeds, return policies, warranties, and post-sales service – that can elevate the price. But even if the product comes in at a slightly higher-than-average price, it can still be a more desirable choice when the retailer supplements that price with better delivery terms, longer warranties, and easier returns.

Loyalty matters, too. For years, retailers have pursued customer relationships in a variety of ways – apps, loyalty programs, personalized offers, email marketing, and more. Those investments aren’t irrelevant, of course, but conversational shopping introduces a different starting point. Instead of opening the retailer’s familiar app, a consumer starts with a need and asks AI to find suitable options. The retailer becomes one of several possible answers, not the default destination.

Consumers remember when a retailer delivers on time, handles a return fairly, or simplifies the checkout process. These thoughtful enhancements to the buying journey create exceptional loyalty and higher levels of trust that AI can’t replicate.

What Retailers Should Do Now

There’s no need to reinvent your entire digital strategy, but there are important steps to take when thinking about how your products appear as consumers use AI to research purchases. Use authentic shopping pathways to test several different AI assistants. What products appear? What information do those assistants use? Are the descriptions, prices, and availability accurate? Note the questions your product pages don’t answer. Keep pricing, promotions, and shipping information current. Determine how to measure visibility when discovery happens outside your channels.

Without question, AI-assisted shopping is still evolving, and even the best assistants can miss relevant products, misunderstand preferences, or present outdated information. But don’t confuse those limitations with any lack of consumer interest. The significant change is that shoppers increasingly begin with a question instead of a destination. The purchase may still happen on a retailer’s website or in its store. The decision about where to spend, however, is increasingly happening elsewhere.

Nicolas Salat-Baroux is one of the 3 co-founders of Joko, alongside Xavier and Alexandre. He currently serves as Chief Revenue Officer (CRO), where he leads the Online, Gift Cards, and Card-Linked business lines, as well as Joko’s partnerships in the U.S. Based in New York, Nicolas brings a business perspective shaped by his previous experience in M&A at Goldman Sachs, and in business development at Jumia across Africa. He is a graduate of ESSEC Business School. Passionate about retail innovation, Nicolas is on a mission to build the ultimate AI shopping app, that helps consumers find the right product for them and buy it at the best price.

data.title: AI Agents Are Browsing. Ahead of Black Friday, Retailers Need Them to Buy
data.description:
Retailers are racing to win agentic attention ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday. The question they should be asking is whether they can convert that attention into actual sales.

Every retail conversation seems to have a new audience: agents. The advice is familiar by now. Structure your product data so large language models can find it, understand it and recommend it. Let’s imagine the strategy works. Your product appears in an AI-generated answer. A shopping assistant visits your site, compares products, creates an account, or moves toward a transaction. You’ve captured a new kind of attention.

Then what? Are you ready to receive the traffic you’ve worked so hard to attract?

Attention Is Not the Same as Readiness

The first mistake is to assume agentic attention behaves like human attention.

A human visitor arrives with a browser, a device, a set of intentions and a degree of context that retailers have spent decades learning to interpret. An agent may arrive on behalf of a person, another system or no legitimate customer at all. It may be gathering information, comparing options, executing a task, testing a credential or probing for a weakness.

From the outside, those interactions can look remarkably similar. That is the central tension in the agentic internet: the traffic that looks like a promising new customer may also be automated abuse wearing the shape of a promising new customer.

The question is not simply whether an interaction claims to be ChatGPT, Claude or another recognized agent. Names and user-agent strings are not identity. They can be copied, manipulated or used as camouflage. A request presenting itself as a familiar AI assistant may be a legitimate agent acting for a real buyer. It may also be a spoofed system, a scraper or a fraud operation using AI because it knows businesses are eager to welcome machine-driven demand.

And the landscape is already more varied than the phrase “AI agent” suggests. Cloud agents, agentic browsers and browser extensions can all reach the same digital property, sometimes through nearly indistinguishable paths.90% of agentic traffic observed by HUMAN is stealth by default. The traffic does not arrive carrying a reliable badge that tells a retailer what it is, who authorized it or what it intends to do.

Influencing an Order Is Not the Same as Completing One

Salesforce reported that AI and agents influenced 20% of all global orders during Cyber Week 2025. That number has shaped a lot of planning for this season, and the verb matters: influencing an order and completing one are not the same thing.

DoorDash offered the clearest illustration. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call, CEO Tony Xu was asked about agent-based ordering. His answer: “we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents.” Several hundred, at a company that completes roughly three million deliveries a day.

That tracks with what latest trends in agentic traffic: across September, 60.4% of agentic activity went to ecommerce sites, 81% of it landed on search and product pages, and 2.4% reached checkout. Meta’s Muse, which arrived at number one in its first month, sent 76.5% of its traffic to ecommerce and converted 2.6% of it.

So agents are arriving in volume and browsing intensively, but they are very rarely buying. For retailers heading into Black Friday and Cyber Monday, that gap is the whole story, because agentic traffic is already shaping the numbers you use to judge performance without showing up in the revenue those numbers are meant to explain. Page views inflate. Measured conversion falls. Neither movement tells you anything about demand.

Routing Matters More Than Welcoming

The next phase of agentic commerce will not be defined by whether retailers let automated traffic in. It will be defined by whether they can route different kinds of traffic intelligently.

Different participants need different experiences:

  • A human buyer may need a rich, persuasive journey
  • A legitimate agent may need clear product data, structured policies, inventory information and a reliable path to act on its user’s behalf
  • A training crawler may be governed by a content-access policy
  • A suspicious interaction may deserve additional verification
  • A malicious operation should be stopped

This is why “block or allow” is becoming an inadequate operating model. It treats every automated interaction as interchangeable at exactly the moment automation is becoming more diverse, more commercially important and harder to distinguish by appearance alone.

It also requires marketing, security and fraud teams to share more than a meeting. Without shared definitions and shared accountability, marketing celebrates a surge in agentic traffic that security experiences as an attack wave.

Four Actions for Retailers Before Black Friday

None of this has to wait for a new platform or budget cycle.

  1. Establish a baseline now, while the week is still ordinary. If you don’t know what share of your traffic is agentic today, you will have nothing to read your Cyber Week numbers against.
  2. Separate agentic activity in your reporting rather than letting it blend into the totals, so conversion and engagement stay interpretable when volume spikes.
  3. Decide in advance which agents get which access, and be specific: browsing, account creation, authentication, checkout. Those are different permissions, and peak week is a poor time to be making the call live.
  4. Agree who owns the decision when marketing and security disagree. That conversation is uncomfortable in November and nearly impossible in December.

The Takeaway

Traditional retail metrics were built around human visibility. Sessions, add-to-carts and conversion rates remain useful, but become harder to read when a growing share of activity is mediated by an agent. A page view may be a crawler collecting competitive pricing. A completed transaction may be legitimate commerce, an unauthorized purchase, or a test of stolen payment credentials.

Being mentioned by an AI system isn’t the same as being chosen by a customer, and being chosen by an agent isn’t the same as being ready to serve, verify and retain the customer behind it.

In the agentic internet, attention is only the beginning. The advantage will belong to the retailers who can recognize what arrives, route it responsibly, convert it safely and tell the difference between activity and growth.

Sarah Acker is SVP and Global Head of Marketing at HUMAN Security, where she leads worldwide marketing strategy spanning brand, creative, communications and product marketing. She writes regularly on agentic traffic, measurement and digital trust.
data.author: Sarah Acker, SVP and Global Head of Marketing, HUMAN Security

data.title: The Holiday Support Spike Isn’t a Staffing Problem. It’s a Repetition Problem.
data.description:
Why Shopify merchants are rethinking post-purchase support before the next peak hits

Every ecommerce team knows the pattern. Traffic climbs, orders land, and within days the inbox fills with the same handful of questions: Where is my order? Can I change my address? What’s your return policy? Does this come in another size?

The instinctive response is to hire seasonal agents, extend hours and hope the queue holds. But the questions behind the spike are rarely new. They are the same ones answered thousands of times, and each one costs as much to answer in November as in March.

The Real Cost Sits After the Checkout

Retailers have spent a decade optimizing everything before the “Buy” button: ads, landing pages, checkout flow. Post-purchase is where the margin quietly leaks. A shopper who has paid and now waits for an answer is at their most anxious and their most loyal-or-lost.

For Shopify merchants the problem is sharper. The platform makes it easy to launch fast and scale quickly, but support rarely scales with the storefront. A lean team that handled 50 orders a day comfortably is suddenly handling 500, with the same two people and the same help desk.

Why Legacy Chatbots Didn’t Fix It

Rule-based bots promised relief but delivered rigid decision trees, dead-end flows and a “talk to a human” button that appeared too late. What has changed is that automation can now be trained on the merchant’s own knowledge, such as help center, FAQs, policies and past conversations, rather than a script.

It can answer in your terms, not generic ones.

A Different Model: AI That Knows the Business and Knows When to Step Aside

This is the approach behind VivoChat, an AI customer support platform built for online businesses. Instead of a fixed flow, the assistant is trained on a merchant’s documents, FAQs, help center content and previous conversations. It answers repetitive questions around the clock, collects the data a human agent will need, and hands complex cases to a person with the context already attached.

For ecommerce teams, three capabilities matter most:

  • Fewer “where is my order” tickets. Connecting shipping tools lets the assistant answer WISMO questions directly instead of routing them to an agent.
  • Support that sells. A shopping assistant can recommend products and suggest relevant add-ons in the same conversation where a shopper is already asking questions.
  • Subscription-aware answers. For subscription brands, integrations with tools such as Recharge, Skio and Loop let the assistant handle common subscription requests.

Conversations also don’t stay trapped on the website. VivoChat covers site chat, email, WhatsApp, Instagram and Messenger, so customers can reach a brand where they already are.

Built to fit a Shopify Stack

For merchants, the practical barrier to AI support is often implementation time. VivoChat is available through the Shopify App Store and is designed to install without code, so a small team can get running before the next promotion instead of after it.

According to VivoChat, merchants can automate up to 70% of repetitive conversations from day one, with the assistant resolving up to 53% of support requests and an average first response time of around 30 seconds. VivoChat also cites support cost reductions of up to 50%. Results will vary with catalog complexity, policy clarity and the quality of the knowledge the assistant is trained on.

Support is Becoming a Team of Agents, Not a Single Bot

A second shift raises the stakes. Shoppers increasingly start with an AI assistant instead of a search bar, asking it to compare products or summarize return policies before they ever reach a store. Those assistants will read what a merchant publishes, so policies buried in PDFs and contradictory FAQs now hurt twice: once with shoppers, and again when an AI misreads them.

It also changes what support automation should mean. Retail support is really several jobs, from pre-sale questions and order status to billing, onboarding and retention, each with its own data, rules and escalation paths. VivoChat‘s answer is an agent marketplace: alongside the core assistant, businesses can install specialized agents published by partners for billing, onboarding, sales and retention. A Shopify merchant can start with order status and FAQs, then add a retention agent ahead of a subscription push.

The benefit is focus. A narrowly scoped agent is easier to test, easier to trust and easier to hand off to a human, so support grows in modules as the business does, instead of in headcount.

What to Do Before the Next Peak

Whatever tool a retailer chooses, the planning question is the same. Instead of asking “how many agents do we need for peak?”, ask “which of our tickets should never need an agent?”

  1. Audit your top 20 ticket types. Most teams find the majority are repetitive and answerable from existing content.
  2. Fix the source material first. An assistant is only as accurate as the help center, policy pages and FAQs behind it. Treat that content as infrastructure.
  3. Define the handoff. Decide which cases, such as refunds above a threshold, damaged goods or VIP customers, always go to a human.
  4. Measure beyond deflection. Track resolution quality, repeat contacts and revenue influenced, not only ticket volume.

Peak season will keep testing support teams. The merchants who handle it best won’t necessarily be the ones with the biggest bench of agents. They will be the ones that stopped paying humans to answer the same question for the thousandth time.

Merchants can also add specialized agents from the VivoChat marketplace, for billing, onboarding, sales and retention. VivoChat is available in the Shopify App Store and installs without code. data.title: How AI Is Reshaping the 2026 Holiday Shopping Journey: What SMBs Need to Know
data.description:
A few years ago, holiday shopping felt pretty predictable. Black Friday arrived, shoppers got serious, and businesses kicked their holiday marketing into high gear.

That timeline has changed.

Nearly half of shoppers planned to start their holiday shopping before November last year, with 11% planning to begin as early as September. And they aren’t shopping in just one place. Last holiday season, 64% of U.S. shoppers blended searching, scrolling, streaming and shopping throughout the customer journey.

Now, AI is adding another stop to that journey.

AI Offers Shopping Personlization

Nearly 40% of consumers are open to using tools like ChatGPT to help with their holiday shopping this year. Instead of Googling “gifts for Dad” and opening a dozen tabs, a shopper can now ask an AI tool something like, “What should I get my dad who loves fishing, already owns every fishing gadget imaginable and is impossible to shop for? My budget is $75.” Suddenly, the shopper has a personalized list of ideas without doing nearly as much searching herself.

For small and medium-sized businesses, that may sound like one more thing to worry about this holiday season. It doesn’t have to be. The fundamentals of good marketing haven’t disappeared. SMBs just need to start a little earlier and make sure those fundamentals work in a shopping journey that now includes AI.

First, Make Your Business Easy to Understand

The number one rule in marketing is to know your audience and meet them where they are. In 2026, some of those customers are increasingly discovering products through AI-assisted search. That makes the information on your website more important, not less.

Imagine you sell a holiday coffee gift set. One product description says: Holiday Gift Set: $39

Another says: Holiday coffee gift set featuring two locally roasted blends and a ceramic mug. Arrives in gift-ready packaging, with free local pickup available.

Which one gives a shopper more confidence? The second description gives search engines and AI tools more context about what you actually sell, who might want it and when it could be relevant.

Go through your website the way a holiday shopper would. Is it easy to find your prices? What comes with the product? Who is it ideal for? Can it be personalized? How long does shipping take? Is local pickup available?

And don’t forget the questions your customers ask you every day. Those FAQs make great website content because chances are, if one customer is asking, another one is searching for the same answer. Clarity matters even more when shoppers are watching their budgets. Sixty-one percent of U.S. shoppers say they have become more selective about spending, and consumers are 1.7 times more likely to purchase from brands they trust.

Make it easy for them to understand why you’re worth choosing.

September: Get the Foundation Ready

One of the biggest holiday marketing mistakes SMBs make every year is treating November like the starting line. By November, you should be running your holiday strategy, not figuring out what it is. September is the time to get your digital storefront ready.

Review your website on your phone. Update product and service descriptions. Confirm pricing and inventory. Make sure your Google Business Profile and other online listings have accurate information. Think through holiday hours, shipping deadlines and pickup options.

This is the time to decide what you actually want to promote.

That doesn’t automatically mean a discount. Maybe your local coffee shop creates a Holiday Morning Kit with coffee, locally made biscotti and a handwritten gift tag. Maybe your salon creates a gift-card bundle. Maybe your bakery brings back the peppermint brownies customers start asking about every October.

Holiday shoppers are looking for value, but value doesn’t always mean “cheapest.” Convenience, personalization, gift-ready packaging, local pickup and great service can all help a small business stand out.

October: Start Showing Up

October is when I’d start building visibility. Publish the gift guide. Introduce your holiday products. Email your existing customers. Start posting on social media. Begin testing paid campaigns. Ask happy customers for reviews.

And yes, this is a great time to use AI to make some of that work easier. Generative AI can help a busy business owner brainstorm blog topics, create a content calendar, draft an email, repurpose that email into social posts or organize FAQs for a holiday landing page.

The important part is not letting AI turn your business into everybody else’s business. If you ask an AI tool to “write a holiday post for my bakery,” you may get something like:

Make this holiday season unforgettable with our curated selection of festive treats.

It sounds perfectly nice. It could also belong to a bookstore, hair salon or, with a few tweaks, probably a plumber. Instead, give AI something real to work with:

We’re a family-owned bakery. Our peppermint brownies have sold out every December for 14 years, and customers start asking about them in October. Write a warm Instagram post reminding people to preorder.

Now AI has your actual business to work with. Use your products, customer questions, employees, traditions, deadlines and personality in your prompts. AI can help create the content, but you still need to provide the part that makes it yours.

November: Stop Planning and Start Executing

By November, your holiday machine should be moving. Your Black Friday and Cyber Monday promotions should be ready. Holiday shipping deadlines should be visible. Your email and social calendars should already exist. Your inventory plan should be in place. And remember that holiday marketing doesn’t end on Cyber Monday.

The message simply changes.

Early in the season, you might be helping customers brainstorm gifts. Later, the questions become: Will it arrive in time? Can I pick it up locally? Do you sell gift cards? What can I get for the person I forgot was coming to dinner?

Those are marketing opportunities, too. If your last day for guaranteed Christmas delivery is December 18, say it clearly. Put it on your website. Put it in your email. Put it on social media. Don’t make a stressed holiday shopper hunt for basic information.

AI May Change Discovery. Trust Still Wins the Sale.

There’s a lot changing about the holiday shopping journey, and AI will undoubtedly play a bigger role in how customers discover and compare businesses.

But I wouldn’t throw out the holiday marketing playbook. Customers still want useful information. They still read reviews. They still care about value. They still want to know that the business on the other side of the screen is one they can trust.

SMBs don’t need to chase every new AI trend this holiday season. Start early. Make your business easy to understand. Give customers the information they need to confidently choose you. And use AI where it genuinely saves you time without letting it replace the personality that made customers choose your small business in the first place.

AI may be changing how the holiday shopping journey begins. The part where a business earns the customer’s trust is still very human.

Alicia Pringle is Senior Director of Online Marketing at Network Solutions, where she leads a global team specializing in SEO, paid search, social media, content and digital marketing services for small businesses. She focuses on helping SMBs adapt to changes in search, AI-powered discovery and customer behavior while keeping practical, customer-first marketing at the center of their strategies.
data.author: Alicia Pringle, Senior Director of Online Marketing at Network Solutions

data.title: Your Customers Don’t Think in Channels—and Neither Should Your Marketing Team
data.description:
Consumers do not think in channels. They do not categorize a promotional email as “digital” and a catalog arriving at their home as “offline.” They simply experience the brand.

Retail marketing organizations often operate differently. Email, paid social, search, and direct mail may be managed by separate teams, supported by different agencies, and measured against different objectives. Each group optimizes its own channel, but most are not necessarily looking at how those interactions fit together from the customer’s perspective.

The answer is not adding more channels or increasing message frequency. It is using customer behavior to coordinate when and how each channel appears.

Start With The Customer, Not The Channel

Traditional campaign planning often begins with a channel-specific question: What should we send to our email list? Who should receive the next catalog? How should we allocate the paid social budget?

An integrated strategy starts with a different question: What is the customer signaling, and how should the brand respond? Someone who browses a product several times without purchasing may need more information or a stronger incentive. A customer who abandons a cart may benefit from a reminder. A previously loyal customer whose purchasing has slowed may need to be reintroduced to the brand.

These are customer situations, not channel assignments. Once marketers understand the situation, they can determine the right touchpoint. Email may quickly deliver an offer. Paid social can keep a product visible. A targeted postcard can provide a physical reminder that remains in the home after a digital impression disappears.

Let Digital Behavior Inform Physical Outreach

Online behavioral signals can also make physical outreach more timely and relevant. Website visits, product-category interest, email engagement, cart activity, and purchase history can indicate where a customer is in the decision process.

A triggered postcard might follow a period of online browsing without conversion, reinforce a promotion introduced through email, or reengage someone whose purchase history suggests they may be ready to buy again.

In this role, direct mail acts as a chaser to digital activity, extending the conversation through a format with different strengths. Sending the same promotion through every available channel is not integration. Each touchpoint should serve a specific purpose based on what the customer has already seen or done.

Build One Message Across Multiple Touchpoints

Customers should not encounter one offer in their inbox, another on social media, and an unrelated message in the mail. That does not mean every execution should look identical. A social video, email, and postcard require different creative approaches. But the central message, product focus, and next action should feel connected.

If paid social introduces a product, email might provide additional details or reviews. Direct mail could reinforce the brand and its value with a strong visual and a reason to act. Each interaction advances the story rather than starting it over.

This coordination can also prevent overcommunication. When teams share a unified plan, they can determine whether a customer actually needs another message or has already received enough contact.

Measure The Journey, Not Individual Victories

Silos are reinforced when teams are evaluated only on channel-specific metrics. Email focuses on opens and clicks. Paid media tracks impressions and attributed conversions. Direct mail measures response rates. Each channel can appear successful without answering the larger question: Did these efforts work better together?

Brands should examine how customers exposed to different combinations of channels behave compared with appropriate control groups. Did customers who received email and direct mail convert at a higher rate than those who received email alone? Did a physical reminder accelerate a purchase or increase order value?

Attribution will never be perfect, but control groups, suppression testing, and overlap analysis can provide a more credible view than evaluating channels in isolation. The goal is not to determine which channel deserves the credit. It is to understand which sequence of interactions moves the customer forward.

Organize Around The Customer Journey

Technology can connect customer data and automate campaign triggers, but it cannot fix a disconnected planning process. Email, paid media, creative, analytics, and direct mail teams need shared objectives and a process for coordinating campaigns.

Consumers have already integrated their shopping behavior. They may discover a brand through a catalog, research a product online, stay engaged on social media, and ultimately act after receiving a postcard or clicking an email link. To them, these are not separate marketing channels; they are all part of one relationship with the brand.

Marketing organizations need to operate with that same mindset. The question should not be which channel drove the sale, but whether each interaction made the next one more relevant and effective. When teams plan around customer behavior rather than channel boundaries, digital and physical marketing can work together as one connected experience.

Your customers are not thinking about your channel strategy. They are thinking about your brand. Your marketing should feel just as seamless to them as it does.

Donna Belardi is a seasoned marketing executive and entrepreneur with more than 30+ years of experience driving growth for premium retail and consumer brands. As Chairman and CEO of Belardi Wong, she co-founded and built the firm into one of the industry’s most respected marketing partners, evolving it from a catalog-focused business into a fully integrated, data-driven agency serving more than 300 leading brands.
data.author: Donna Belardi, CEO and Chairman of Belardi Wong

data.title: Gopuff Offers Weekly Pokémon Trading Card Drops, Delivered in Minutes
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Gopuff will drop Pokémon Trading Card Game products every Friday at 3 p.m. ET for six weeks, with delivery in as fast as 15 minutes and one below-market “Hit of the Week” card from Card Vault by Tom Brady.
  • Trading card sales on Gopuff climbed 335% from Q4 2025 to Q3 2026, prompting the company to turn high-demand launches into scheduled shopping events.

Gopuff, the leader in instant commerce, today launched a new drop feature offering high-demand, limited-quantity products at a set time, delivered in as fast as 15 minutes.

The weekly drops hat began Nov. 6  brings Pokémon Trading Card Game packs to the platform, giving collectors nationwide access to some of the hobby’s most sought-after cards alongside their groceries, snacks and everyday essentials.

The launch builds on growing demand for trading cards on Gopuff. Since the category debuted on the platform, trading card sales have climbed 335% from Q4 2025 to Q3 2026, signaling rising interest from collectors looking for a fast and convenient way to get the cards they want.

Why Is Gopuff Launching Scheduled Product Drops?

“Our goal is to make Gopuff the fastest way to get the internet’s most-wanted products,” said Tyler Stewart, Head of Marketing at Gopuff.

“Our new drops give people something to look forward to, from the anticipation to the reveal, with a few surprises along the way,” said Stewart in a statement. “And the best part? No lines, no waiting for shipping. Just the products you want, delivered in minutes. We’re excited to continue building on this experience, with more iterations to come.”

How Do Gopuff’s Weekly Pokémon Card Drops Work?

Gopuff will drop Pokémon Trading Card Game products every Friday at 3:00 p.m. ET for six consecutive weeks. The lineup will feature collector favorites like the Mega Evolution—Pitch Black Elite Trainer Box and the 30th Celebration Poster Collection, all available at competitive prices. Quantities are limited and products are available on a first-come, first-served basis, so once a drop sells out, it’s gone.

Each drop will also feature a “Hit of the Week,” presented in partnership with Card Vault by Tom Brady. Every Friday, customers will have the chance to purchase a high-value Pokémon card at a price well below market value. With just one available each week, customers will want to check Gopuff right at 3:00 p.m. ET for their chance to snag it and shop the latest drop.

Each week of the campaign follows the same schedule:

  • Monday: A countdown clock appears on the Gopuff homepage, building anticipation for Friday’s drop. The products remain a mystery, giving customers a teaser that another drop is on the way.
  • Thursday at 3:00 p.m. ET: 24 hours before the drop, Gopuff reveals the products that will be available. Customers can then set an alert to receive a notification as soon as the drop goes live and dd products to their cart ahead of time so they’re ready to check out when the drop begins.
  • Friday at 3:00 p.m. ET: The drop goes live and checkout opens, allowing customers to complete their purchases while supplies last.

What Features Come With Each Gopuff Drop?

Designed to make shopping for high-demand products easier and more accessible, Gopuff’s drops turn product launches into scheduled shopping events, giving fans a new way to get their hands on some of the internet’s most sought-after products.

Each drop features, a dedicated storefront. alerts and add-to-cart options and Rapid local delivery as orders can be fulfilled from nearby Gopuff micro-fulfillment centers for delivery in as fast as 15 minutes.

Available while supplies last with quantities varing by location and purchase limits may apply. Customers can shop Gopuff’s assortment at www.gopuff.com or in the Gopuff app on iOS and Android.
data.author: james.hickey
